column2: Cloud computing is the delivery of computing services over the internet. These services can include servers, storage, databases, networking and software. Instead of buying and maintaining all the physical equipment yourself, you can use resources provided by a cloud service provider. This can help an organisation access technology quickly and adjust its resources as its needs change. For example, a business experiencing more online orders during a promotion can increase its computing capacity without permanently purchasing additional servers.

The shared responsibility model explains how security and management duties are divided between a cloud provider and its customer. The provider is responsible for some parts of the cloud infrastructure, while the customer remains responsible for other areas. The exact division depends on the cloud service being used. Customers commonly need to manage their data, identities, access permissions and appropriate configurations. Moving an application to the cloud does not remove the customer's responsibility to protect its information and control who can access it.

Cloud deployment models describe how cloud resources are made available. A public cloud provides services over the internet using infrastructure operated by a cloud provider. A private cloud is dedicated to a single organisation and may be hosted by that organisation or a provider. A hybrid cloud combines public and private cloud environments, allowing an organisation to use both. Each model has different implications for control, management and flexibility. Choosing a model depends on the organisation's requirements, including security, workload needs and how it wants to manage its resources.

Different cloud models suit different organisational needs. A public cloud can be useful when an organisation wants to deploy services quickly and scale resources without managing its own physical infrastructure. A private cloud may suit workloads that need more direct control over the environment. A hybrid cloud can help an organisation keep some workloads in a private environment while using public cloud resources for other workloads or periods of increased demand. The best choice depends on the organisation's technical, security, operational and business requirements rather than one model being best for every situation.

The consumption-based model means that customers pay for cloud resources based on their usage, according to the service's pricing rules. They can avoid buying as much physical infrastructure upfront and can adjust their resource usage as demand changes. For example, a business may use more computing capacity during a busy season and reduce its usage afterward. This flexibility can help control costs, but it does not mean every cloud service is free of fixed charges or commitments. Customers should monitor their usage and understand the pricing terms of each service.

Cloud pricing models vary according to the service, usage pattern and commitment made by the customer. Pay-as-you-go pricing allows customers to pay for eligible resources as they use them. Some services also offer commitment-based options that can reduce costs when a customer commits to using eligible resources for a specified period. The most suitable option depends on how predictable the workload is and whether the commitment matches actual demand. Before choosing a pricing model, compare its conditions, flexibility and potential savings, and check the provider's current pricing information.

Serverless computing lets developers run code or build applications without having to manage the underlying servers directly. The cloud provider manages much of the server infrastructure, allowing developers to focus more on application logic. Serverless does not mean that servers do not exist; it means that server management is abstracted from the developer. For example, Azure Functions can execute code in response to events, such as a timer or an incoming request. Depending on the service and plan, billing may be based on executions and resource consumption.
